title: The Murle Through Sudan's Civil Wars
subtitle: The Murle experience of the First and Second Sudanese Civil Wars, political division, survival and the road to peace
author: Murle Connect

body.heading: The Murle and the Beginning of Sudan's Civil Wars
paragraphs: The history of the Murle people during Sudan's civil wars cannot be separated from the wider political history of southern Sudan. The wars were not simply conflicts between ethnic groups. They were also struggles over political power, representation, land, resources, religion, regional autonomy and the relationship between the southern peoples and the government in Khartoum.

The Murle entered these conflicts as a distinct people with their own traditional institutions, political interests and relationships with neighbouring communities. Different Murle communities and leaders did not always make the same political choices.

This distinction is essential. During the civil wars, some Murle supported southern rebel movements, some fought alongside government forces or government-backed militias, and others attempted to protect their communities independently. The choices changed over time according to local circumstances.

body.heading: The First Sudanese Civil War
paragraphs: The First Sudanese Civil War began in 1955, shortly before Sudan became independent in 1956. It developed from longstanding political and military tensions between the northern and southern parts of Sudan.
The conflict continued until the Addis Ababa Agreement of 1972. During these years, southern communities experienced military campaigns, displacement, insecurity and political instability.

The Murle were affected by the wider war, but their experience was also shaped by their particular position in the eastern part of southern Sudan. Their relations with the government and with neighbouring communities influenced how different Murle leaders responded to the conflict.

The First Civil War established patterns that would become important during the Second Civil War: the arming of local communities, the use of ethnic and regional alliances, mistrust between neighbouring peoples and the increasing militarization of southern society.

body.heading: Murle Political Choices During the First War
paragraphs: The Murle did not act as a single political or military organization throughout the First Civil War. Some Murle individuals participated in the southern resistance, while others developed relationships with the Sudanese government.
One important example was Hassan ŋacingol, who became the first Murle to serve as a District Commissioner and later aligned himself with the Sudanese government during the Anyanya period.

Such political choices should be understood within the circumstances of the time. The Murle were dealing with pressure from the government, neighbouring communities and local insecurity, while also attempting to preserve their own communities and political interests.
The later history of the Murle demonstrates why it is inaccurate to describe the entire people as permanently belonging to one side of Sudan's civil wars.

body.heading: The Addis Ababa Agreement and the Years of Relative Peace
paragraphs: The First Civil War ended with the Addis Ababa Agreement in 1972. The agreement provided southern Sudan with regional self-government and brought a period of relative peace.

For communities such as the Murle, the agreement created an opportunity to rebuild after years of conflict. People could return to communities affected by war, restore cattle herds and agricultural activities, and rebuild social institutions.
The peace, however, did not resolve all of the political disagreements between the southern region and the Sudanese central government.

By the early 1980s, the political settlement was breaking down. The division of the southern region, disputes over autonomy and the growing power of the central government created the conditions for a new war.

body.heading: The Second Sudanese Civil War Begins
paragraphs: The Second Sudanese Civil War began in 1983 after the collapse of the Addis Ababa settlement. The Sudan People's Liberation Movement and Sudan People's Liberation Army, led by John Garang, emerged as the principal southern rebel movement.
The war eventually became one of Africa's longest and most destructive conflicts. It lasted from 1983 until the signing of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement in January 2005.

The conflict transformed political and social life across southern Sudan. Communities were displaced, towns changed hands, weapons became widespread, and local conflicts increasingly became connected to the larger war.
The Murle homeland became strategically important because of its location near the Ethiopian border and because of the road and river routes connecting different parts of eastern southern Sudan.

body.heading: The 1983 Mutiny at Pibor
paragraphs: The beginning of the Second Civil War was closely connected to military mutinies in southern Sudan. In 1983, soldiers at Pibor, Bor and other locations resisted orders from the Sudanese government.
The Pibor mutiny became an important part of the wider chain of events that led to the formation and expansion of the SPLA.

The participation of soldiers from the Pibor area demonstrated that Murle communities were not outside the southern political struggle. Murle individuals were among those who became involved in the emerging southern rebellion.
At the same time, the subsequent relationship between the SPLA and different Murle communities became increasingly complicated.

body.heading: Boma and the SPLA
paragraphs: Boma became one of the important early strongholds of the SPLA. The highland location was strategically significant because of its proximity to Ethiopia and its position overlooking the surrounding lowlands.

The SPLA maintained a major base in Boma for much of the Second Civil War. Many highland Murle remained associated with the movement, and Boma became one of the places through which the SPLA projected military and political influence into the wider region.
The importance of Boma during the war created a different political experience from that of many lowland Murle communities around Pibor.
This difference later became one of the reasons that the wartime history of Boma Murle and Pibor Murle must be discussed separately without treating them as separate peoples.

body.heading: The Growing Murle–SPLA Tension
paragraphs: Although some Murle joined the SPLA, support for the movement declined among many Murle after abuses, killings and political grievances affected relations between the community and the rebel movement.
Some Murle believed that the SPLA's leadership structure was dominated by larger southern groups and that the interests of smaller communities such as the Murle were not adequately protected.

The killing of prominent Murle figures and other experiences of violence contributed to growing distrust. These developments did not end Murle participation in the SPLA, but they helped create a widening political divide.
The result was not a simple Murle-versus-SPLA conflict. Some Murle continued to serve within the SPLA while others increasingly looked for their own means of community defence.

body.heading: Ismael Konyi and the Pibor Defence Force
paragraphs: One of the most important figures in the wartime history of lowland Murle was Sultan Ismael Konyi.

Before the Second Civil War, Konyi had organized Murle youth for community policing and local security. When the rebellion began in 1983, this organization developed into the Pibor Defence Force, commonly known as the PDF or locally as the Brigade.

The PDF was a Murle armed organization based primarily in the Pibor area. Its stated purpose was to defend Murle communities and territory against external threats, particularly the SPLA and attacks associated with neighbouring communities.

The Sudanese government in Khartoum supported Konyi's forces with weapons, uniforms and ammunition because the PDF could help oppose the SPLA in an area where the government had difficulty maintaining direct control.

body.heading: Why Konyi Aligned With Khartoum
paragraphs: Konyi's alliance with Khartoum should be understood within the political circumstances of the war rather than as evidence that all Murle supported the Sudanese government.

For Konyi and many of his supporters, the immediate concern was the security of the Murle community in the Pibor area. The SPLA was increasingly viewed by some lowland Murle as a threat, while neighbouring Dinka and Nuer communities were also involved in the wider armed conflict.

Khartoum therefore became a source of weapons and political support for a local Murle defence organization. The alliance was useful to the Sudanese government because it placed a local armed force against the SPLA.

This arrangement also had long-term consequences. After the war, the relationship between Konyi's forces and Khartoum contributed to widespread suspicion of Murle by sections of the SPLM/A and the new South Sudanese state.

body.heading: Pibor Under the Pibor Defence Force
paragraphs: Pibor became one of the most important areas of confrontation between the SPLA and forces aligned with Konyi.

The SPLA controlled or maintained a strong presence in Boma, while Pibor remained largely outside SPLA control for much of the war. According to conflict research, Pibor was under Sudanese government garrison control for much of the Second Civil War, apart from a shorter period of SPLA control between approximately 1987 and 1992.
In 1992, Konyi's forces took control of Pibor town and maintained their position there for much of the remaining war.
This created a striking political geography: Boma became strongly associated with the SPLA, while Pibor became strongly associated with Konyi's forces and the Sudanese government alliance.

body.heading: The Murle Were Not One Side
paragraphs: The wartime division within Murle society is one of the most important facts to preserve when writing Murle history.

Highland Murle in Boma included many people associated with the SPLA. Lowland Murle around Pibor included many supporters of Konyi and the Pibor Defence Force. Other Murle served in different forces or attempted to remain outside the main military organizations.
These political divisions did not create different Murle peoples. Families, clans, age-sets, language and cultural institutions continued to connect people across the divide.
The civil war therefore divided political loyalties more than it erased Murle identity.

body.heading: War and Relations With Neighbouring Communities
paragraphs: The civil war also transformed relationships between the Murle and neighbouring Dinka and Nuer communities.

Weapons supplied by the Sudanese government, the SPLA and other armed actors became increasingly available to local communities. Cattle raids and local conflicts therefore became more destructive because traditional forms of conflict were increasingly connected to modern firearms and wider military alliances.

The war also encouraged governments and armed movements to describe local communities according to political categories. Communities that supported one side could be treated as enemies by the other side.
This created a cycle in which political conflict, cattle raiding, revenge attacks and military alliances reinforced one another.

body.heading: Displacement and the Destruction of Rural Life
paragraphs: The civil wars disrupted ordinary Murle life across the homeland. Families were displaced from villages and cattle camps, agricultural production was interrupted, and access to grazing areas and water became more uncertain.
People also moved across borders and between the lowlands and highlands in response to insecurity.

Children grew up during years in which armed conflict was part of everyday life. Schools and health services were extremely limited in many parts of the region, while humanitarian assistance became increasingly important.
Despite these conditions, Murle communities maintained family relationships, age-set identities, clan institutions, cattle traditions, agriculture and oral history.

body.heading: The 1991 SPLA Split and Its Effects
paragraphs: The SPLA itself experienced a major internal split in 1991. The division involved leading commanders including Riek Machar and Lam Akol and created another period of intense fighting across parts of southern Sudan.
The split had serious consequences for Jonglei and surrounding regions. Large numbers of people were displaced, and conflicts between Dinka, Nuer and other communities became increasingly severe.

Pibor also became a destination for some people fleeing the fighting elsewhere in Jonglei. At the same time, relations between sections of the Murle and Nuer population deteriorated as local attacks and cattle raids intensified.
The 1991 split therefore added another layer to an already complicated regional conflict.

body.heading: The Murle and the Human Cost of War
paragraphs: The Murle experienced the civil war both as participants in armed organizations and as civilians caught between competing forces.

Villages and cattle camps could become targets because of their perceived political loyalties. Civilians could be displaced by fighting, lose livestock or agricultural land, and face shortages of food and medicine.
The wider Second Civil War caused enormous loss of life across southern Sudan. Millions of people were killed, displaced or affected by famine, disease and conflict.
The Murle experience must therefore be placed within the wider suffering of southern Sudan while also recognizing the specific political and geographical circumstances of the Pibor region.

body.heading: The Changing Position of Ismael Konyi
paragraphs: As the Second Civil War continued, Konyi remained one of the most important Murle political and military figures in the Pibor region.

His relationship with Khartoum became an important part of the political history of the lowland Murle. At the same time, the wartime division did not prevent all communication between different Murle communities.

By the end of the war, the political environment had changed significantly. The southern movement and the Sudanese government were moving toward negotiations, while armed groups across southern Sudan faced the question of what would happen to their forces after peace.
Konyi's later decision to align with the emerging South Sudanese political order demonstrated that wartime alliances could change when the political situation changed.

body.heading: The Comprehensive Peace Agreement
paragraphs: The Second Sudanese Civil War ended with the signing of the Comprehensive Peace Agreement on 9 January 2005.
The agreement created a new political framework for southern Sudan, including a period of autonomous government and provisions for a referendum on self-determination.

For the Murle, the end of the war created both hope and uncertainty. Armed groups had to consider integration, disarmament and political participation, while communities that had fought on different sides had to live within the same emerging political system.

The peace agreement also exposed unresolved problems. Weapons remained widespread, relations between neighbouring communities remained tense, and the legacy of wartime alliances continued to influence political attitudes.

body.heading: Murle Forces After the Peace Agreement
paragraphs: After the 2005 peace agreement, many former armed groups were faced with the choice of integrating into the Sudan People's Liberation Army, joining other security structures or maintaining their own forces.
Konyi eventually moved toward cooperation with the SPLM-led government in southern Sudan and officially aligned with the SPLA in the post-war period.

The integration of former opponents was not immediate or complete, however. Some former fighters and commanders retained independent loyalties, while others continued to be associated with the Sudanese Armed Forces or other political networks.

The process illustrates one of the central difficulties of post-war South Sudan: peace agreements could end the major national war without immediately removing the local conflicts, weapons and mistrust that the war had created.

body.heading: The Legacy of the Civil Wars
paragraphs: The civil wars left a deep mark on Murle political history. The division between Boma and Pibor during the Second Civil War became part of later political narratives about Murle loyalty and security.

The association of many lowland Murle with Konyi and Khartoum was later used by some political actors to portray the Murle as unreliable or hostile to the southern movement. Such interpretations were too broad because many Murle had fought within the SPLA and many others had not participated directly in armed politics.

The wars also changed the relationship between Murle communities and neighbouring Dinka and Nuer populations. Weapons, displacement and wartime alliances intensified conflicts that had previously been more localized.
At the same time, the wars strengthened the political importance of Pibor and Boma and helped shape later demands for greater local autonomy and self-government.

body.heading: The Road From War to South Sudan
paragraphs: The end of the Second Civil War opened a new chapter in Murle history. The 2005 peace agreement created the political conditions that eventually led to the 2011 referendum and the independence of South Sudan.
Murle communities entered this new period carrying the experiences of two major civil wars, displacement, political division and armed self-defence.

The post-war period would bring new opportunities for political participation, but it would also bring new disputes over disarmament, representation, security and relations with neighbouring communities.
The history of the civil wars therefore did not end in 2005. Its political and social consequences continued to influence Murle life after the birth of South Sudan.

body.heading: One People Through a Divided War
paragraphs: The most important lesson from the Murle experience of Sudan's civil wars is that political division did not destroy the underlying unity of the Murle people.

Murle men and women fought on different sides, lived in different wartime zones and experienced different relationships with the SPLA and the Sudanese government. Boma and Pibor followed different political paths, and individual leaders made different choices.
Yet the Murle continued to share language, ancestry, clans, age-sets, traditional institutions and a connection to the same wider homeland.

The civil wars therefore belong to Murle history not only as a story of armed conflict, but also as a story of survival. Communities adapted to changing governments, armies and borders while preserving the cultural institutions that connected them across the highlands and lowlands.
By 2005, the war that had divided Sudan was ending. For the Murle, however, a new chapter was beginning: the struggle to define their place within the emerging state of South Sudan.

timeline.event: The First Sudanese Civil War begins.
Sudan becomes independent while the southern conflict continues.
Murle communities experience the wider Anyanya-era conflict and changing relationships with the Sudanese government.
The Addis Ababa Agreement ends the First Sudanese Civil War and establishes southern regional self-government.
The Addis Ababa settlement collapses and the Second Sudanese Civil War begins. Mutinies occur at Pibor and other southern military locations.
Boma becomes an important SPLA stronghold, while political relations between the SPLA and many lowland Murle become increasingly strained.
Ismael Konyi develops the Pibor Defence Force as a Murle armed organization aligned with the Sudanese government.
Pibor experiences a period of SPLA control during the Second Civil War.
The SPLA split intensifies conflict and displacement across Jonglei and surrounding areas.
Konyi's forces take control of Pibor town, which remains largely outside SPLA control for much of the remaining war.
Wartime alliances, displacement, cattle conflict and local insecurity intensify across Jonglei.
The Comprehensive Peace Agreement ends the Second Sudanese Civil War.
Former armed groups begin processes of integration and political realignment while wartime mistrust remains.

historicalNote: The Murle were not politically united on one side during Sudan's civil wars. Some Murle participated in or supported the SPLA, particularly in Boma, while many lowland Murle around Pibor were associated with Sultan Ismael Konyi's Pibor Defence Force, which received support from the Sudanese government. Pibor was a government-aligned stronghold for much of the Second Civil War, while Boma remained an important SPLA base. These wartime divisions were political and military divisions within one Murle people, not evidence of separate Murle ethnic groups. Accounts of wartime violence should also be read carefully because different communities remember and interpret these events differently.
